# PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor

###### Abstract

Existing methods for AI psychological counselors predominantly rely on
supervised fine-tuning using static dialogue datasets. However, this
contrasts with human experts, who continuously refine their proficiency
through clinical practice and accumulated experience. To bridge this
gap, we propose an Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent
(PsychAgent) for psychological counseling. First, we establish a
Memory-Augmented Planning Engine tailored for longitudinal multi-session
interactions, which ensures therapeutic continuity through persistent
memory and strategic planning. Second, to support self-evolution, we
design a Skill Evolution Engine that extracts new practice-grounded
skills from historical counseling trajectories. Finally, we introduce a
Reinforced Internalization Engine that integrates the evolved skills
into the model via rejection fine-tuning, aiming to improve performance
across diverse scenarios. Comparative analysis shows that our approach
achieves higher scores than strong general LLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4,
Gemini-3) and domain-specific baselines across all reported evaluation
dimensions. These results suggest that lifelong learning can improve the
consistency and overall quality of multi-session counseling responses.

## 1 Introduction

Psychological counseling remains difficult to access in many settings
because demand for mental-health support exceeds the supply of qualified
professionals. Recent large language models (LLMs), including foundation
models such as GPT-4o ([1](#bib.bib1)), Llama ([2](#bib.bib2)), and
DeepSeek ([3](#bib.bib3)), have shown strong semantic understanding,
making them promising for tasks ranging from empathetic support to
preliminary psychological assistance.

In response, the research community has increasingly specialized LLMs
for mental health. Early efforts, such as ChatCounselor ([4](#bib.bib4))
and SoulChat ([5](#bib.bib5)), used domain-specific fine-tuning to
improve professional capability and emotional resonance. More recent
work has moved toward agent-based systems with stronger clinical
structure. For example, AutoCBT ([6](#bib.bib6)) employs multi-agent
collaboration to deliver structured Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, while
PsyDT ([7](#bib.bib7)) introduces “Digital Twins” to model the
personalized styles of specific therapists. Addressing the temporal
dimension, MusPsy ([8](#bib.bib8)) emphasizes the importance of
multi-session tracking. However, many of these systems remain largely
static after training: whether relying on fixed weights or pre-defined
workflows, they provide limited support for updating strategies from
ongoing interactions.

This static paradigm stands in stark contrast to the professional growth
of human counselors. A human therapist does not become an expert solely
by studying textbooks or datasets; rather, they cultivate expertise
through an experience-driven loop by accumulating “clinical intuition”
from years of successful and unsuccessful cases. This discrepancy
suggests three key challenges in current AI counseling: 1) unlike human
experts who refine techniques and abstract practical skills from
experience, many SFT-based models remain fixed after training and do not
update their strategies from interaction history; 2) counseling is
inherently longitudinal, and human counselors rely on long-term memory
and strategic planning to guide clients over weeks or months, whereas
current models often lack persistent context for multi-session
coherence; 3) human experts gradually transform accumulated knowledge
into more internalized abilities that can transfer across scenarios,
while existing models often depend on external retrieval or rigid
prompts, with limited evidence that these learned behaviors are
reflected more directly in model parameters.

To address this gap, we propose an Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning
Agent (PsychAgent) for AI psychological counseling. Drawing inspiration
from how human counselors improve through practice, our framework
combines a Memory-Augmented Planning Engine for longitudinal continuity,
a Skill Evolution Engine for extracting practice-grounded therapeutic
skills from historical counseling trajectories, and a Reinforced
Internalization Engine for integrating these evolved skills into model
parameters via rejection fine-tuning. Experimental results show that
PsychAgent achieves higher scores than strong general LLMs (e.g.,
GPT-5.4 ([9](#bib.bib9)), Gemini-3 ([10](#bib.bib10)) and
domain-specific baselines, supporting the usefulness of learning from
accumulated counseling experience.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose PsychAgent, which, to our knowledge, is among the first
  frameworks to formulate AI psychological counseling as an
  experience-driven lifelong learning problem, loosely inspired by the
  professional development of human counselors.
- •
  We design a Memory-Augmented Planning Engine for longitudinal
  continuity, and a Skill Evolution mechanism combined with Reinforced
  Internalization to enable the autonomous discovery and assimilation of
  therapeutic skills. Extensive experiments show that our approach
  achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating superior
  generalization and consistency in providing professional counseling
  services compared to existing methods.
- •
  Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art
  performance, demonstrating superior generalization and consistency in
  providing professional counseling services compared to existing
  methods.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 LLMs for Psychological Counseling

Recent work has adapted LLMs to mental-health support and psychological
counseling through domain-specific data and supervision. Early efforts
such as ChatCounselor ([4](#bib.bib4)), Psy-LLM ([11](#bib.bib11)),
SoulChat ([5](#bib.bib5)), and MindChat ([12](#bib.bib12)) mainly
improve empathy, emotional support, and counseling-oriented dialogue
generation. Subsequent work injects stronger therapeutic structure into
the model or system design, for example through cognitive
reframing ([13](#bib.bib13)), CBT-grounded modeling ([14](#bib.bib14),
[15](#bib.bib15)), multi-agent coordination ([6](#bib.bib6)), or
therapist-style modeling via digital twins ([7](#bib.bib7)). In
parallel, evaluation has become more systematic, covering counseling
competency, therapy-specific ability, and ethical
risks ([16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)), together
with broader human-evaluation frameworks for healthcare
LLMs ([19](#bib.bib19)).

A parallel line of work emphasizes that counseling is inherently
longitudinal rather than single-turn. MusPsy ([8](#bib.bib8)),
PsyDial ([20](#bib.bib20)), and PsychEval ([21](#bib.bib21)) move toward
multi-session data and evaluation, while TheraMind ([22](#bib.bib22))
incorporates cross-session planning and adaptation into the agent
itself. However, these systems are still largely static after training:
they may better model history or follow structured workflows, but they
do not explicitly extract new therapeutic skills from accumulated
interactions and internalize them into model parameters. Our work
targets this gap by framing AI psychological counseling as an
experience-driven lifelong learning problem.

### 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning

The evolution of Continual Learning (CL) has undergone a paradigm shift,
transitioning from merely mitigating catastrophic forgetting in static
architectures to enabling dynamic adaptation in LLMs ([23](#bib.bib23)).
Traditional approaches largely addressed the stability-plasticity
dilemma through regularization techniques like EWC ([24](#bib.bib24)) or
experience replay mechanisms ([25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26)). While
recent frameworks have introduced sophisticated memory
management ([27](#bib.bib27)) and reinforcement
learning ([28](#bib.bib28)) to handle long-term interactions, they
predominantly focus on data retention rather than high-level skill
acquisition, often struggling with the semantic complexity of open-ended
real-world tasks ([29](#bib.bib29)).

Building on this direction, recent work has increasingly explored
Self-Evolving Agents that refine capabilities through recursive loops of
experience and reflection ([30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31)).
Frameworks such as SAGE ([32](#bib.bib32)) and
Richelieu ([33](#bib.bib33)) suggest that agents can improve reasoning
through self-reflective critique. However, many existing systems still
rely heavily on transient in-context learning or external retrieval
(RAG) to exhibit “growth.” As formalized by Cai et
al. ([34](#bib.bib34)), Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning (ELL)
ideally requires agents to autonomously acquire, refine, and use skills
from dynamic environments. In this work, we apply this perspective to
psychological counseling by modeling a cycle of accumulating clinical
experience, abstracting therapeutic skills, and internalizing them
through training.

![Refer to caption](2604.00931v3/Framework.png)

Figure 1: The overall architecture of PsychAgent, an experience-driven
lifelong learning framework for psychological counseling. The system
operates through a synergistic closed-loop mechanism: (a) The
Memory-Augmented Planning Engine ensures therapeutic continuity across
longitudinal sessions by reasoning over dynamic client profiles and
formulating strategic goals; (b) The Skill Evolution Engine manages a
hierarchical repository of therapeutic techniques, supporting both
real-time context-aware retrieval and the post-session abstraction of
novel skills; (c) The Reinforced Internalization Engine solidifies these
capabilities via rejection fine-tuning, where optimal trajectories are
selected to transform explicit skills into the model’s endogenous
intuition.

## 3 Our Methods

As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor"),
we propose PsychAgent, an experience-driven framework intended to
capture aspects of how counselors improve through practice. The
architecture includes three components: the Memory-Augmented Planning
Engine, which supports therapeutic continuity across longitudinal
sessions through long-term context; the Skill Evolution Engine, which
extracts successful intervention strategies into a structured
hierarchical skill tree; and the Reinforced Internalization Engine,
which incorporates these explicit skills into model parameters via
rejection-based reinforcement. By iterating over these stages,
PsychAgent is designed to reduce reliance on static imitation and heavy
external retrieval.

We formulate the AI psychological counseling task as a Lifelong
Sequential Decision-Making problem, where an agent $`\pi_{\theta}`$
interacts across a longitudinal timeline
$`\mathcal{T}=\{S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{T}\}`$. For each session $`S_{t}`$,
the agent generates a response trajectory conditioned on the evolving
client state $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ (Memory) and a dynamic repository of
therapeutic strategies $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$ (Skills). The overarching
objective is to maximize the cumulative therapeutic effectiveness
$`\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{R}(S_{t})`$ through an iterative closed-loop
process: intra-session, the agent utilizes a Memory-Augmented Planning
Engine and a Skill Evolution Engine to retrieve explicit knowledge for
immediate reasoning; inter-session, the agent employs a Reinforced
Internalization Engine to lock in the optimal trajectory
$`S_{t}^{*}`$—identified via rejection sampling from parallel
rollouts—thereby continuously updating its parameters $`\theta`$ to
internalize successful clinical experiences.

### 3.1 Memory-Augmented Planning Engine

Standard LLMs often suffer from temporal incoherence in long-context
interactions, failing to maintain a consistent therapeutic trajectory.
To mitigate this, the Memory-Augmented Planning Engine
(Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")a)
serves as the agent’s cognitive substrate, ensuring longitudinal
continuity. This engine is designed to support longitudinal continuity
through three functions: Dynamic Memory Construction, Strategic
Planning, and Context-Aware Generation.

#### Dynamic Memory Construction.

Unlike static context windows, we maintain a structured memory store
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ that evolves alongside the therapy. This is composed
of two parts:

- •
  Evolving Client Profile ($`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$): Rather than a fixed
  intake form, the client profile is treated as a dynamic semantic
  memory. At the conclusion of each session $`S_{t-1}`$, the agent
  explicitly extracts new attributes (e.g., changes in family status,
  new medical diagnoses) to incrementally refine the profile:

  |     |     |     |     |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  |     |

  ````math
  \mathcal{P}_{t}\leftarrow\text{Update}(\mathcal{P}_{t-1},\text{Extract}_{\text{attr}}(S_{t-1}))
  ``` |  | (1) |

  This helps the agent maintain an updated understanding of the client’s
  life circumstances.
  ````

- •
  Episodic Session Summaries ($`\mathcal{H}_{t}`$): To compress
  long-term history, the agent generates a structured summary
  $`h_{t-1}`$ of the previous interaction, capturing key emotional
  shifts and intervention outcomes, which is appended to the history:
  $`\mathcal{H}_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{t-1}\cup\{h_{t-1}\}`$.

#### Goal-Oriented Strategic Planning.

Therapy requires foresight. Before initiating session $`S_{t}`$, the
engine performs Plan Reasoning to synthesize the updated memory
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}=(\mathcal{P}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t})`$ into a coherent
roadmap. The model predicts a structured plan $`G_{t}`$,
encompassing: 1) Therapeutic Stage: Identifying the global phase (e.g.,
Case Conceptualization, Core Intervention, Consolidation and
Prevention); 2) Session Objectives: Formulating specific, actionable
goals for the current session (e.g., “Reinforce cognitive restructuring
techniques”). This planning step provides a more structured framework
for subsequent dialogue generation, rather than leaving the interaction
purely reactive.

To endow the agent with these capabilities, we construct high-quality
instruction data $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y)\}`$ for each sub-task and train
the model to minimize the negative log-likelihood across all tasks:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=-\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{plan}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{resp}}}\log P_{\theta}(y|x)
``` |  | (2) |

Specifically, the training corpus is constructed to cover the core
stages of the counselor’s cognitive workflow, mapping distinct inputs
$`x`$ to targeted outputs $`y`$ across three tasks: for Memory
Extraction (($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{mem}}`$)), the model learns to distill
raw dialogue history into structured profile updates and session
summaries; for Plan Reasoning ($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{plan}}`$), it learns
to translate the accumulated memory state $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ into
strategic goals $`G_{t}`$; and for Response Generation
($`\mathcal{D}_{\text{resp}}`$), it conditions on memory, plan, and user
input ($`(u_{i},\mathcal{M}_{t},G_{t})`$) to jointly generate
chain-of-thought reasoning $`z_{i}`$ and the final therapeutic response
$`r_{i}`$. Explicit supervision of these steps is intended to improve
the model’s structured counseling decision-making.

### 3.2 Skill Evolution Engine

While the Memory Engine anchors the agent in the client’s past, the
Skill Evolution Engine
(Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")b)
is designed to expand the model’s explicit repository of therapeutic
techniques over time. Unlike static systems relying on fixed prompt
engineering, this engine maintains a dynamic ontology of therapeutic
techniques. We unify both the utilization and evolution of skills under
a generative framework, acquired through rigorous Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT) on expert-annotated cognitive tasks.

#### Hierarchical Skill Taxonomy.

We formalize the skill knowledge base as a hierarchical tree structure
$`\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{E})`$, where nodes $`\mathcal{N}`$
represent therapeutic skills organized into four granular levels:

- •
  Root Paradigms ($`n_{root}`$): The foundational counseling frameworks
  that define the theoretical basis (e.g., CBT, Humanistic Therapy).
- •
  Therapeutic Stages ($`n_{stage}`$): The macro-phases of the counseling
  process, specifically defined as Case Conceptualization, Core
  Intervention, and Consolidation and Prevention.
- •
  Meta Skills ($`n_{meta}`$): High-level strategic categories nested
  within each stage (e.g., Empathy Building in the conceptualization
  phase).
- •
  Atomic Skills ($`n_{atomic}`$): Concrete, executable intervention
  tactics used in single turns (e.g., “Socratic Questioning,”
  “Metaphorical Reflection”).

#### Context-Aware Skill Retrieval.

During inference, the agent must select the optimal intervention
strategy $`\kappa^{*}`$ from the skill tree $`\mathcal{T}_{t}`$ to guide
the current response. This is modeled as a context-dependent generation
task. Given the current dialogue state
$`s_{t}=(u_{i},\mathcal{M}_{t},G_{t})`$, the model computes the
probability of selecting specific atomic skills:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\kappa^{*}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\kappa\in\mathcal{N}_{atomic}}P_{\theta}(\kappa|u_{i},\mathcal{M}_{t},G_{t})
``` |  | (3) |

The retrieved skill $`\kappa^{*}`$ is then explicitly prepended to the
generation context (visualized as the \<skill\> token), serving as a
high-level directive for the subsequent response $`r_{i}`$.

#### Generative Skill Evolution.

A key capability of the Skill Evolution Engine is its ability to update
the skill tree after each session through a hierarchical, reflective
process. This is enabled by fine-tuning the model on two specialized
tasks designed to enforce structural consistency:

- •
  Targeted Skill Extraction: rather than generic abstraction, the
  evolution is anchored in the session’s therapeutic goal. The model
  first retrieves the most relevant Meta-Skill ($`M`$) aligned with the
  session goal. It then analyzes the high-reward trajectory $`S^{*}`$ to
  abstract a specific Atomic Skill ($`\kappa_{atom}`$) that instantiates
  this meta-strategy:

  |  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  \kappa_{atom}\leftarrow\mathcal{E}_{\theta}(S^{*}\mid M,\text{Goal})
  ``` |  | (4) |

  This ensures that new skills are categorized under the correct
  pedagogical branch.
- •
  Adaptive Skill Management: To maintain an efficient knowledge base,
  the model performs a context-aware update within the identified
  Meta-Skill branch. It retrieves the existing atomic skill
  ($`\kappa_{ref}`$) most semantically similar to $`\kappa_{atom}`$. The
  model then executes a decision policy $`\pi_{mgmt}`$ to either append
  the new skill as a distinct node or merge it with the existing one to
  refine the definition:

  |  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  \mathcal{T}_{t+1}\leftarrow\begin{cases}\mathcal{T}_{t}\cup\{\kappa_{atom}\}&\text{if }\pi_{mgmt}(\kappa_{atom},\kappa_{ref})=\text{Append}\\
  \text{Merge}(\mathcal{T}_{t},\kappa_{ref},\kappa_{atom})&\text{if }\pi_{mgmt}(\kappa_{atom},\kappa_{ref})=\text{Merge}\end{cases}
  ``` |  | (5) |

  This mechanism prevents redundancy while allowing the continuous
  refinement of existing techniques.

Analogous to the optimization strategy employed in the Memory module, we
construct specialized SFT data to equip the agent with these
evolutionary capabilities. Through this targeted fine-tuning, PsychAgent
learns to autonomously curate its own professional knowledge base,
realizing true open-ended learning.

### 3.3 Reinforced Internalization Engine

While the Skill Evolution Engine expands the agent’s explicit knowledge
base, the Reinforced Internalization Engine
(Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")c)
focuses on transforming this external knowledge into endogenous
intuition. To achieve this, we employ an iterative Rejection Fine-Tuning
(RFT) mechanism ([35](#bib.bib35)), which mimics the human process of
reflecting on and reinforcing successful counseling experiences while
discarding ineffective ones.

#### Iterative Trajectory Rollout and Selection.

Unlike standard reinforcement learning that explores at the token level,
our engine performs exploration at the session level to ensure coherent
long-term strategies. As illustrated in the bottom panel of
Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor"),
the process unfolds iteratively for a sequence of sessions:

- •
  Parallel Rollout: At any session step $`t`$, given the history of the
  previous optimal sessions $`\mathcal{H}^{*}_{t-1}`$, the agent
  generates $`N`$ parallel candidate sessions
  $`\{S_{t}^{(1)},\dots,S_{t}^{(N)}\}`$. Each candidate explores
  different combinations of retrieved skills and dialogue strategies.
- •
  Reward Evaluation: We employ a comprehensive Reward Model to assess
  the quality of each completed session candidate, denoted as
  $`S_{t}^{(k)}`$. To capture the complexity of real-world counseling,
  the evaluation metric $`\mathcal{R}`$ is designed as a holistic
  integration of client- and counselor-centric dimensions using
  LLMs-as-a-Judge ([36](#bib.bib36)), following ([21](#bib.bib21)). The
  final reward score serves as a critical feedback signal, guiding the
  model toward strategies that are both clinically valid and
  psychologically supportive.
- •
  Greedy Selection: We select the optimal session $`S_{t}^{*}`$ that
  yields the maximum reward:
  $`S_{t}^{*}=\operatorname{argmax}_{k}\mathcal{R}(S_{t}^{(k)})`$.
  Crucially, the memory state for the subsequent session $`t+1`$ is
  updated based only on this optimal trajectory $`S_{t}^{*}`$. This
  ensures that the agent’s lifelong learning path is constructed solely
  from its most successful interactions (marked with trophies in
  Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2.2 Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")).

#### Internalization via Rejection Fine-Tuning.

After constructing the optimal lifelong trajectory
$`\mathcal{T}^{*}=\{S_{1}^{*},S_{2}^{*},\dots,S_{T}^{*}\}`$, the engine
utilizes this data for parameter optimization. We treat the rejected
sessions (those with lower rewards, marked with crosses) as negative
samples implicitly. The model is fine-tuned to maximize the likelihood
of the selected ”golden” trajectory $`\mathcal{T}^{*}`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{RFT}(\theta)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_{\theta}(S_{t}^{*}|\mathcal{H}^{*}_{t-1})
``` |  | (6) |

Through this process, the explicit skills and planning logic used to
generate $`S_{t}^{*}`$ are gradually ”distilled” into the model’s
weights $`\theta`$. Over time, this allows PsychAgent to produce
high-quality responses intuitively, reducing its dependence on heavy
external retrieval.

## 4 Experimental Results

### 4.1 Experimental Setups

#### Datasets and Metrics.

We build our experiments on PsychEval ([21](#bib.bib21)). Following its
protocol, we first perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the released
multi-session counseling corpus, and then reuse its pool of 2,000+
client profiles for both rollout training and evaluation. For each
therapeutic school, we sample 140 client profiles, using 120 for
training and 20 for evaluation. We adopt the evaluation protocol of
PsychEval. Across all therapeutic schools, we report the shared
counseling metrics, including PANAS, RRO, SRS, Custom_Dim, HTAIS, WAI,
and Dialogue_Planning. In addition, each school is evaluated with two
school-specific metrics: behavioral therapy with MITI and STAI,
cognitive-behavioral therapy with CTRS and BDI_II, postmodernist therapy
with EFT_TFS and SFBT, humanistic-existential therapy with TES and CCT,
and psychodynamic therapy with PSC and IPO. Following PsychEval, we
report both counselor-side and client-side results, further organized
into therapy-shared and therapy-specific dimensions.

#### Baselines.

We compare PsychAgent against two categories of baselines to disentangle
the effects of general reasoning ability and domain-specific counseling
specialization. For General-purpose LLMs, we include several strong
off-the-shelf LLMs: GPT-5.4 ([9](#bib.bib9)),
Gemini-3 ([10](#bib.bib10)), Qwen3-Max ([37](#bib.bib37)), and
DeepSeek-V3.2 ([38](#bib.bib38)). These baselines represent
state-of-the-art general models and allow us to assess whether strong
counseling performance can be achieved from general capability alone.
For Psychology-Specific LLMs, we include PsyLLM ([11](#bib.bib11)),
PsyDTLLM ([7](#bib.bib7)), CPsyCounX ([39](#bib.bib39)), and
TheraMind ([22](#bib.bib22)). PsyLLM incorporates explicit diagnostic
and therapeutic reasoning, PsyDTLLM models counselor-specific style via
digital twins, CPsyCounX is fine-tuned on reconstructed counseling
dialogues, and TheraMind is designed for longitudinal counseling with
cross-session planning and adaptation.

#### Implementation Details.

We finetune PsychAgent with Qwen3-32B and set the maximum context length
to 32,768 tokens. All models are trained with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 in bf16
precision, using a per-device batch size of 1, gradient accumulation of
8, a learning rate of $`1\times 10^{-5}`$, cosine decay, and 10% warmup
for 3 epochs. The rollout number $`N=8`$. History masking is enabled in
all experiments unless otherwise specified. Training is conducted on two
servers, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

### 4.2 Main Results

As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setups ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor"),
PsychAgent achieves higher scores than both general-purpose and
psychology-specific baselines across all four aggregated evaluation
dimensions. Compared with the strongest general-purpose baseline,
Qwen3-Max, PsychAgent improves counselor-level shared/specific scores by
+1.44/+0.17 and client-level shared/specific scores by +0.51/+0.43.
Relative to the longitudinal counseling agent TheraMind, the
corresponding gains are +1.07, +0.97, +0.44, and +0.41 on the four
dimensions. These results suggest that strong general reasoning or
longitudinal planning alone may not fully account for high counseling
performance on this benchmark.The gains remain substantial against the
longitudinal counseling agent TheraMind, with improvements of +1.07,
+0.97, +0.44, and +0.41 on the four dimensions. These results suggest
that the observed gains are not explained solely by domain adaptation or
cross-session planning. Notably, even PsychAgent^(†) (8B) achieves the
best or second-best result on every dimension, which suggests that the
improvements are associated with the proposed lifelong learning
framework in addition to model scale.
Figure [3](#A0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
in the appendix further suggests that the gains are broad-based rather
than concentrated in only one or two metrics. The largest improvements
appear on counselor-side planning and intervention measures, including
Dialogue_Planning (9.41 vs. 6.52) and CTRS (9.41 vs. 7.96), consistent
with stronger session structuring and more theory-aligned interventions
under this benchmark. Meanwhile, steady gains are also observed on
client-side outcomes such as CCT (8.13 vs. 7.04) and SFBT (6.71 vs.
5.57), suggesting that the benefits of the framework are reflected not
only in counselor behavior but also in client-side outcome measures.
Overall, these results are consistent with effective counseling in this
benchmark benefiting from both longitudinal context handling and
continued skill evolution/internalization.

### 4.3 Human Evaluation

To complement automatic evaluation, we conduct human expert evaluation
on multi-session counseling dialogues generated by PsychAgent,
Qwen3-Max, and TheraMind. Each dialogue is independently rated by two
human annotators and one LLM rater (Gemini-3) on four dimensions Ethics,
Interaction, Intervention, and Perception using a 1–5 ordinal scale, and
we report Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) ([40](#bib.bib40)) to measure
agreement. Across 522 matched dialogues, PsychAgent is ranked first by
both human raters and the LLM rater, suggesting that its relative
advantage is not limited to automatic metrics. Meanwhile, annotator
agreement is moderate to strong: human–human agreement reaches 0.675
QWK, while the LLM rater attains higher agreement with the two human
raters (0.770 and 0.877), suggesting that it may serve as a useful
auxiliary evaluator in this setting. Due to space constraints, the
annotation guidelines, annotation details, and detailed analyses of the
evaluations are provided in
Section [B](#A2 "Appendix B Human Evaluation ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
of the appendix.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Human Evaluation ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
suggests that all three components contribute to the final performance
of PsychAgent. Removing any module consistently lowers both
counselor-level and client-level results, which is consistent with the
overall gains arising from their combination. Among them, removing the
Skill Evolution Engine (SEE) leads to the largest drop in this ablation,
suggesting that skill evolution may be the most influential component
under the current setting. Removing the Reinforced Internalization
Engine (RIE) also causes noticeable performance loss, indicating that
retrieved skills benefit from further internalization. Removing the
Memory-Augmented Planning Engine (MAPE) results in a smaller but still
consistent decline, highlighting the contribution of longitudinal memory
and session-level planning. Overall, the results suggest that strong
psychological counseling requires not only memory, but also skill
acquisition and internalization from experience.

### 4.5 Further Analysis

Figure 2: Clients’ Emotional Trajectories.

#### Analysis of Clients’ Emotional Trajectories.

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.5 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
compares the session-wise client trajectories across models. In Panel
(A), where lower values are better, PsychAgent shows a relatively
pronounced downward trend, suggesting a larger reduction in negative
client states over time. In Panel (B), where higher values are better,
it remains above the compared baselines across much of the trajectory
and improves steadily across sessions. Relative to the flatter or less
stable trajectories of other models, these patterns are consistent with
more stable multi-session performance, although they should be
interpreted as benchmark trends rather than direct clinical evidence.

Table 4: Influence of Memory Mechanisms.

#### Influence of Memory Mechanisms

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Analysis of Clients’ Emotional Trajectories. ‣ 4.5 Further Analysis ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
suggests that simply adding existing memory architectures to a strong
backbone such as DeepSeek-V3.2 yields limited benefit for this
benchmark, and in some cases slightly lowers performance. This pattern
indicates that generic memory methods, including Vanilla
RAG ([41](#bib.bib41)), Graph RAG ([42](#bib.bib42)),
Mem0 ([43](#bib.bib43)), and MemoryBank ([44](#bib.bib44)), may be
insufficient on their own for this setting. One possible explanation is
that counseling requires more than recalling past facts: the model may
also need to track evolving mental states, therapeutic progress, and the
rationale behind prior interventions. In contrast, PsychAgent achieves
higher scores across all metrics, which is consistent with the value of
combining memory with skill learning and internalization.

#### Case Studies

To better understand why PsychAgent improves counseling performance, we
examine representative cases of skill extraction and
post-internalization behavior (Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Case Studies ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")).
Three observations are particularly notable. First, the model often
distills practice-grounded skills from counseling trajectories rather
than merely restating entries in the initial skill library, which is
consistent with a form of self-evolution from practice (Section
[C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Extracting New Skills from Conversations ‣ Appendix C Case Studies ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")).
Second, after internalization, the model often combines existing
micro-skills into *new functional skills* rather than only reusing
predefined ones, suggesting a degree of skill-level compositional
reorganization beyond the original inventory (Section
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Operational New Functional Skills ‣ Appendix C Case Studies ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")).
Third, some internalized skill packages recur across therapeutic
orientations, suggesting partial cross-context reuse of intervention
patterns rather than strict therapy-specific reuse only (Section
[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Cross-Therapy Reuse ‣ Appendix C Case Studies ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")).
Taken together, these findings indicate broader functional reuse, though
not therapy-agnostic counseling.

## 5 Conclusions and Further Work

We introduced PsychAgent, an experience-driven lifelong learning
framework for AI psychological counseling that integrates
memory-augmented planning, skill evolution, and reinforced
internalization. By moving beyond static fine-tuning, PsychAgent enables
the counselor agent to improve through accumulated experience and
deliver more consistent, professional, and effective multi-session
support. Experiments across multiple therapeutic schools show that our
framework consistently outperforms both strong general-purpose LLMs and
psychology-specific baselines. Future work will focus on evaluating the
framework in more realistic counseling settings and strengthening safety
and privacy protections for real-world deployment.

## Appendix A Detailed Results Across Counselor- and Client-Level Therapy Metrics

Figure [3](#A0.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
provides a fine-grained comparison across counselor- and client-level
therapy metrics, covering both therapy-shared and therapy-specific
dimensions. Across all four panels, PsychAgent exhibits a consistently
strong performance profile rather than isolated improvements on only a
few metrics. The largest gains appear on counselor-side planning and
intervention dimensions, especially Dialogue_Planning and CTRS,
suggesting stronger ability to structure therapeutic progress and
deliver theory-consistent interventions. Meanwhile, the improvements
also extend to client-side outcome measures such as CCT and SFBT,
indicating that the benefits of the framework are reflected not only in
counselor behavior but also in downstream client-level therapeutic
progress. Overall, the radar plots support the conclusion that the
proposed lifelong learning framework yields broad and coherent
improvements across therapy dimensions, with especially clear advantages
on metrics that depend on accumulated therapeutic skills and their
effective deployment in ongoing dialogue.

## Appendix B Human Evaluation

### B.1 Raters and Annotation Protocol

We conducted human evaluation on multi-session counseling dialogues
generated by PsychAgent, Qwen3-Max, and TheraMind. The two human raters
were graduate students with psychology-related training, and the third
evaluator was LLM Rater (Gemini-3). All three raters evaluated the
*counselor’s performance*, rather than the client’s state, on four
dimensions: Ethics, Interaction, Intervention, and Perception. All
scores were assigned on a 1–5 ordinal scale. Because these labels are
ordered categorical variables, we report Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK)
as the primary agreement metric; QWK is more appropriate than unweighted
agreement measures because it accounts for the ordinal distance between
adjacent scores.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The matched evaluation set contains 522 fully rated dialogues from 25
cases and 188 case-session units. This yields 6,264 dimension-level
observations and 2,088 paired ratings for each rater pair. One dialogue
was excluded because all three rating files failed for the same item,
leaving a nearly complete matched sample. The sample is balanced across
counselor models (173 PsychAgent dialogues, 175 Qwen3-Max dialogues, and
174 TheraMind dialogues), which supports comparison at the overall,
by-dimension, by-model, and model-by-dimension levels.

### B.2 Inter-Rater Agreement

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
shows that all three raters concentrate heavily on high scores, with 4–5
accounting for 78.8%–81.7% of all dimension-level ratings. This
indicates a generally favorable score distribution and also suggests
some degree of ceiling effect, especially for Perception. Human Rater B
is slightly more lenient than Human Rater A overall, whereas LLM Rater
(Gemini-3) exhibits the largest spread and uses low scores somewhat more
frequently. Nevertheless, the relative ranking of the three counselor
models is remarkably stable across raters: PsychAgent performs best,
Qwen3-Max is consistently second, and TheraMind performs worst.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Level | Group | $`n`$ | Human A vs Human B | LLM vs Human A | LLM vs Human B |
| Overall | All ratings | 2088 | 0.675 | 0.770 | 0.877 |
| By dimension | Ethics | 522 | 0.606 | 0.756 | 0.823 |
|  | Interaction | 522 | 0.576 | 0.691 | 0.841 |
|  | Intervention | 522 | 0.747 | 0.812 | 0.907 |
|  | Perception | 522 | 0.546 | 0.660 | 0.843 |
| By model | PsychAgent | 692 | 0.626 | 0.752 | 0.865 |
|  | Qwen3-Max | 700 | 0.698 | 0.813 | 0.854 |
|  | TheraMind | 696 | 0.528 | 0.649 | 0.821 |

Table 5: Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) across raters.

Agreement results are reported in
Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Inter-Rater Agreement ‣ Appendix B Human Evaluation ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor").
At the overall level, Human Rater A vs Human Rater B achieves a QWK of
0.675, indicating moderately strong agreement. In contrast, LLM Rater
(Gemini-3) attains higher agreement with both human raters: 0.770
against Human Rater A and 0.877 against Human Rater B. Exact agreement
follows the same trend (74.2% for Human A vs Human B, 78.7% for LLM vs
Human A, and 90.3% for LLM vs Human B), and nearly all disagreements are
within one rating point. These results suggest that the LLM rater is not
behaving randomly; rather, it tracks a substantial portion of the human
scoring structure, especially the rating style of Human Rater B.

The agreement pattern is also dimension-dependent. Across all three
pairings, Intervention is the most reliable dimension, reaching QWK
values of 0.747, 0.812, and 0.907. By contrast, Perception shows the
weakest human-human agreement (0.546), and Interaction is also
comparatively variable. This is consistent with the descriptive
distributions: Perception is highly concentrated in the upper score
range, which likely compresses effective variance and makes Kappa
estimates more sensitive to small shifts in rating style.

### B.3 Systematic Bias of the LLM Rater

|              |              |       |                   |                   |
|--------------|--------------|-------|-------------------|-------------------|
| Level        | Group        | $`n`$ | LLM $`-`$ Human A | LLM $`-`$ Human B |
| Overall      | All ratings  | 2088  | $`-0.022`$        | $`-0.043`$        |
| By dimension | Ethics       | 522   | $`-0.031`$        | $`-0.102`$        |
|              | Interaction  | 522   | $`-`$0.025        | $`-0.048`$        |
|              | Intervention | 522   | $`-0.042`$        | $`-0.038`$        |
|              | Perception   | 522   | $`-0.038`$        | $`-`$0.017        |
| By model     | PsychAgent   | 692   | $`-`$0.009        | $`-0.066`$        |
|              | Qwen3-Max    | 700   | $`-`$0.096        | $`-`$0.014        |
|              | TheraMind    | 696   | $`-0.170`$        | $`-0.076`$        |

Table 6: Systematic mean-score bias of LLM Rater (Gemini-3) relative to
each human rater. Positive values indicate that the LLM assigns higher
scores on average.

Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ B.3 Systematic Bias of the LLM Rater ‣ Appendix B Human Evaluation ‣ PsychAgent: An Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning Agent for Self-Evolving Psychological Counselor")
shows that LLM Rater (Gemini-3) does not exhibit a simple global
tendency to inflate scores. Relative to Human Rater A, the overall mean
bias is nearly zero ($`-0.022`$), but this average conceals substantial
model-specific structure: the LLM is slightly more favorable on
PsychAgent and Qwen3-Max, yet clearly harsher on TheraMind ($`-0.170`$).
Relative to Human Rater B, the LLM is more consistently conservative
overall ($`-0.043`$), with its largest dimension-level deviation on
Ethics ($`-0.102`$). Thus, the LLM appears to behave like a relatively
stable additional evaluator whose judgments are closer to Human Rater B
than to Human Rater A, rather than like a neutral proxy for an
underlying gold standard.

Overall, these results suggest that, under a shared and
evidence-grounded rubric, LLM Rater (Gemini-3) provides *substantial
practical reliability* as an auxiliary evaluator in this setting: it
recovers the same model ranking as human raters, achieves high QWK
against both humans, and disagrees mostly by only one rating point.
However, its alignment is not uniform across dimensions or counselor
models. In particular, Ethics, Perception, and lower-performing models
such as TheraMind remain more sensitive to rating-style differences. We
therefore view the LLM rater as a scalable complement to human
evaluation rather than a drop-in replacement for multi-rater human
judgment.

## Appendix C Case Studies

### C.1 Extracting New Skills from Conversations

To better understand why PsychAgent improves counseling performance, we
examine whether its extracted skills merely restate the initial skill
library or instead capture *new practice-grounded skill units* from real
counseling dialogue. Here, we define a practice-grounded skill unit as
an extracted skill that introduces *non-trivial practical increments*
beyond the closest existing micro-skills, rather than simply rephrasing
or elaborating pre-existing entries. Concretely, the comparison baseline
is the v3 library within the same therapeutic orientation and stage,
where micro-skills are already fine-grained and typically include
when_to_use and trigger fields. As a result, a skill is counted as novel
only when it adds practical structure that is not already captured by
the nearest existing micro-skills.

Under this criterion, the answer is clearly positive. Across 715
dialogue records, the extraction pipeline produces 9,701 atomic skills,
among which 5,923 qualify as practice-grounded skill units (B+C). This
pattern holds across all five orientations: the proportion of
practice-grounded skill units reaches 73.29% in BT, 69.77% in CBT, 56.0%
in HET, 51.61% in PDT, and 63.49% in PMT. These results show that the
dominant outcome of extraction is not restatement, but the distillation
of practically enriched skill units relative to the closest existing
micro-skills.

The practical increments are also highly consistent across orientations.
The most frequent additions are clearer operational sequencing, minimum
viable actions, quantitative thresholds, structured templates,
monitoring or recording loops, and pause or rollback rules. In other
words, the model does not mainly invent completely new therapy
techniques; instead, it absorbs interactional experience from counseling
trajectories and re-expresses it as more executable local skill units.
At the same time, our stricter global audit finds no sufficiently
supported candidates for *entirely novel therapy techniques* relative to
the initial library. Even the strongest cases are better understood as
stable repackagings of existing techniques with added thresholds,
templates, monitoring rules, or minimum-action designs.

Representative cases from all five orientations further illustrate this
pattern.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Taken together, these cases clarify what it means for skill extraction
to produce new practice-grounded skill units. The resulting skills are
not merely longer descriptions of existing entries; instead, they encode
interaction-derived thresholds, monitoring rules, minimum viable
actions, sequencing constraints, and reusable templates that are not
fully specified by the closest existing micro-skills. This is why the
strongest supported conclusion is not that the model invents entirely
new therapy techniques, but that it reliably distills practically
enriched skill units from counseling trajectories.

### C.2 Operational New Functional Skills

To better understand why internalization improves counseling
performance, we compare post-internalization behavior against both the
initialized skill library and the SFT baseline. Two observations are
central. First, internalization does not simply increase the number of
multi-skill turns. Instead, it reorganizes existing micro-skills into
more stable and functionally coherent turn-level packages. Second, some
of these internalized packages are reused across therapies, suggesting
that the model acquires transferable counseling principles rather than
only therapy-specific templates. Together, these patterns indicate that
internalization pushes the model toward a more general and versatile
counselor.

The clearest evidence for internalization is not a mechanical increase
in multi-skill turns, but the emergence of recurrent higher-order
packages with clearer local intervention functions. In other words, the
model does not merely place multiple skill labels in the same turn;
rather, it increasingly organizes several existing micro-skills into
compact intervention units that behave like *new functional skills* at
the operational level.

Importantly, these packages should not be interpreted as newly invented
canonical techniques. A more conservative interpretation is that
internalization compresses multiple known micro-skills into recurrent,
stable, and functionally closed turn-level units. This is why the
strongest evidence for compositional generalization comes from the
quality and stability of these packages, rather than from raw bundle
counts alone.

|                                      |         |          |      |        |
|--------------------------------------|---------|----------|------|--------|
| Functional skill                     | Therapy | Internal | SFT  | Status |
| Goal-to-Record Bridge                | CBT     | 30       | 58   | stable |
| Rated Reappraisal Loop               | CBT     | 22       | 104  | stable |
| Dose-Specified Practice Scaffold     | BT      | 18       | 72   | stable |
| Validation-Wrapped Pacing Regulation | PDT     | 6        | 0    | stable |
| Alternative-Story Amplification      | PMT     | 241      | 1338 | stable |
| Resource-to-Action Scaffold          | HET     | 54       | 166  | stable |

Table 8: Representative candidate functional skills after
internalization. These packages are best interpreted as operationally
new functional units built from known micro-skills, rather than as
entirely new canonical techniques.

Across therapies, these cases support the same conclusion: the model
increasingly relies on recurrent functional packages built from existing
skills. This pattern supports a conservative claim of *skill-level
compositional generalization beyond the original inventory*: the model
is not primarily inventing entirely new techniques, but reorganizing
known micro-skills into higher-order functional units with clearer
operational value.

### C.3 Cross-Therapy Reuse

A second important effect of internalization is that some of these
functional packages become reusable across therapies. Here, however, the
strongest evidence does not come from exact cross-therapy bundles within
the same turn, since such strict mixed-therapy combinations remain
limited. Instead, the more informative pattern is *cross-therapy reuse
at the functional-family level*: similar intervention logics recur
across different therapy-specific contexts while preserving related
local counseling goals.

| Affect Attunement Before Deeper Work | CBT, HET, PDT      | 28       | 48   |

Several reusable functional families illustrate the same pattern.
*Goal-to-Practice Bridge* appears across multiple therapies as a shared
logic for translating insight, discussion, or formulation into concrete
between-session action. *Progress Consolidation Package* recurs as a
stable way of summarizing gains, affirming client competence, and
orienting the next phase of work. *Affect Attunement Before Deeper Work*
shows another transferable structure, in which the counselor first
stabilizes or names the client’s emotional experience before moving into
more challenging exploratory work. In each case, what travels across
therapies is not merely a skill label, but an intervention principle.

This distinction is important. The evidence does not support the
stronger claim that internalization turns the model into a fully
therapy-agnostic counselor, nor that it frequently produces large
numbers of exact cross-therapy bundles. What it does support is a more
careful conclusion: internalization enables some higher-order functional
skills to be reused in multiple therapeutic contexts, suggesting that
the model learns counseling principles that are portable beyond a single
therapy-specific template.

Taken together, these findings indicate that internalization improves
both the compositional organization and the portability of counseling
skills. The model becomes better at turning existing micro-skills into
reusable functional units, and some of these units begin to generalize
across therapies. In this sense, internalization moves the model toward
a more general and versatile counselor.
````
